current_answer: U.S. employment in highly AI-exposed occupations weakened again in the Stanford–ADP September payroll update, especially among workers aged 22–30. In its selected firm panel, the high-exposure group fell 0.5% from a year earlier while the least-exposed grew 1.0%; among 22–25-year-olds, the split was −3.7% versus +0.2%. These are observed employment changes by occupation exposure, not AI-caused job losses. German full-time records through 2025 show only a small, statistically uncertain adjusted exposure link for ages 20–29. A four-country study finds remote work weakens the apparent AI link to falling junior hiring shares; newer French records still show an entry-hiring gap. Broad U.S. tracking finds no clear economy-wide AI footprint. A randomized U.S. survey experiment found that a message framing student AI use as replacing learning made hiring professionals rate fictional graduates less favorably, especially high-GPA applicants. It does not show actual callbacks or wages fell. A new U.S. job-ad analysis finds more duty statements classified as new tasks in AI-using occupations, but ads cannot establish new jobs or wages earned. A new Pew U.S. employment analysis finds a within-occupation gender gap that widens with AI task exposure, especially for workers without bachelor’s degrees. This is not evidence that AI caused the gap.

catalogue_card.question: Is AI-exposed work growing equally for women and men?
catalogue_card.text: A U.S. occupation analysis finds slower employment growth for women than men as AI task exposure rises, especially without a bachelor’s degree. It cannot isolate AI as the cause.

summary: Pew finds slower U.S. employment growth for women than men in more AI-exposed occupations, concentrated among workers without bachelor’s degrees; the comparison is not causal.
Newly classified duties in U.S. job ads increased in high-AI-use occupations, but a duty statement is not a completed hire or a new job.

A randomized hiring-vignette study found that framing student AI use as replacing learning lowered stated interview and salary-negotiation ratings for fictional U.S. graduates; it did not observe real hiring.
The September Stanford–ADP payroll update shows a year-over-year employment decline of 3.7% among ages 22–25 in high-AI-exposure occupations versus 0.2% growth in the least-exposed.
The same high-versus-low comparison is −2.8% versus +0.9% for ages 26–30, and −0.5% versus +1.0% across all ages.
The selected firm panel measures occupation exposure, not employer AI adoption or AI-caused layoffs. Remote work remains a competing explanation for part of the junior-hiring pattern.
French permanent-hire flows show a later entry gap; Yale’s broad U.S. tracker still finds no clear economy-wide AI footprint. These sources count different things.
German full-time administrative records through 2025 show a much smaller, statistically uncertain adjusted young-worker exposure association; the sample and period differ from the U.S. panel.
uncertainty: The Canaries September update uses a selected ADP firm panel, excludes firm entry and exit, and groups occupations by exposure rather than actual AI use; it is descriptive, not nationally representative or causal.

Germany’s full-time employee analysis ends in 2025, excludes several worker groups and uses occupation potential rather than actual AI adoption; its adjusted young-worker exposure estimate is not statistically significant.
The remote-work study is observational and ends in 2025; it cannot rule out later or country-specific AI effects.
The French analysis is descriptive and its flows do not measure age-by-occupation employment stocks.
Anthropic is one rapidly growing firm reporting internal, non-audited records.
The Copilot studies use different firm samples and hiring denominators; neither establishes an economy-wide effect.
The adaptive-capacity study combines occupation-level exposure and transition proxies, not observed AI layoffs or realized reemployment.
Occupation averages conceal individual circumstances; future demand may change the ranking.
A new German journal abstract covers mostly pre-generative-AI adoption; its full methods were not accessible.
The sector study uses task exposure rather than observed AI deployment and adjusts a pre-trend in its automatable-task series.
The Argentine experiment took place outside workplaces and did not test actual job access or wages.
The Swedish AI-skill study covers 2014–2023 external hires and excludes ordinary chatbot use; its observational pay gap cannot identify a causal return to training.
The October tracker summary did not expose its full updated data vintage or detailed estimates in the page inspected.
The new hiring-vignette finding concerns opt-in professionals’ hypothetical ratings, not actual callbacks, pay or student AI use.
Only the October new-duty paper’s abstract was accessible; the full classifier tests and sampling detail were not verified, and postings do not show realized work or pay.
Pew’s pre/post CPS comparison uses occupational task exposure, not employer AI adoption, and may reflect other changes.
freshness_note: Checked 28 October 2026. New subgroup evidence changes the scope of the answer; AI causation remains unproven.
